explanations.explanation: Light it is, friend. The Teacher says "…wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). He looks at wisdom and folly side by side and gives wisdom the win. It's like flipping on the kitchen light and finally seeing where the cookie sheet actually is.

Wind does show up in this passage, so I see why it jumped out at you. But that's later, where he calls things "…a pursuit of the wind." (Ecclesiastes 2:17). Here he's comparing wisdom and folly, and he says wisdom exceeds folly "…just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). Light is the winner.

Water makes sense for a comparison, friend, but it's not the one he picks. The Teacher says wisdom exceeds folly "…just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). It's the difference between seeing where you're going and bumping into the oven door.

Close, but the Teacher says the opposite here, friend. He says the wise man has eyes in his head and the fool walks in darkness. Then he adds, "Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both." (Ecclesiastes 2:14). One fate, not two, so the wise man and the fool do not end up with different fates.

False is right, friend. The Teacher first says the wise man has eyes in his head and the fool walks in darkness. Then comes the turn: "Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both." (Ecclesiastes 2:14). The wise man and the fool end up with the same fate, not different ones. I bet that gave him plenty to think about.

explanations.answer: What did being wise gain me
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says to himself, "The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?" (Ecclesiastes 2:15). He's looking at all that wisdom and wondering what it bought him. I think that question sat heavy with him.

The Teacher never says fools seem happier, friend. He's asking about himself. After seeing that the fool's fate will also befall him, he asks, "What then have I gained by being wise?" (Ecclesiastes 2:15). The question is pointed right back at his own wisdom.

explanations.answer: How can I grow even wiser
explanations.explanation: You'd think a wise man would just study harder, wouldn't you? But that's not the question he asks. He says, "What then have I gained by being wise?" (Ecclesiastes 2:15). He turns his question back on the wisdom he already has.

Forgotten, friend. The Teacher says "…there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come." (Ecclesiastes 2:16). Wise or foolish, the remembering fades for both. Every wise man and every fool, same boat.

Praise would be nice, but that's not what the Teacher says. He says "…there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come." (Ecclesiastes 2:16). No lasting remembrance, for the wise or for the fool. Praise isn't in the verse at all.

Envy isn't in this verse, baker. The Teacher says there's no lasting remembrance of the wise or the fool, "…seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come." (Ecclesiastes 2:16). Forgotten is a long way from envied.

He did, friend. The Teacher says plainly, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). That's a heavy thing to say, and I think it hurts to read. The reason he gives is that the work done under the sun was grievous to him.

The Teacher goes the other direction, baker. He says, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). The reason he gives is that the work done under the sun was grievous to him. Loving life even more isn't in the verse.
I'd love to say he laughed, friend, but not this time. The Teacher says, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). This is one of his heavy moments, and I think it hurts to read.

explanations.answer: The work people do was painful to him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. He says, "…I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me." (Ecclesiastes 2:17). The work itself weighed on him. Then he adds, "For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind." (Ecclesiastes 2:17).

explanations.answer: The people he ruled turned from him
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about his people turning from him, friend. He gives his reason: "…the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me." (Ecclesiastes 2:17). The weight came from the work, not from a revolt.

explanations.answer: The enemies he faced took his city
explanations.explanation: No enemies and no lost city here, baker. The Teacher says he hated life "…because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me." (Ecclesiastes 2:17). His trouble is with the work and where it all goes.

explanations.answer: He must leave it to the man after him
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. He says, "I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me." (Ecclesiastes 2:18). All that work, and it goes to someone else. I think that stings.

explanations.answer: It was all taken from him in battle
explanations.explanation: No battle in this verse, baker. The Teacher gives this reason: "…I must leave it to the man who comes after me." (Ecclesiastes 2:18). That's why he hated all he had toiled for. Battle never comes up.

explanations.answer: It had used up all his silver and gold
explanations.explanation: Money running out isn't his complaint, friend. He says he hated all he had toiled for "…because I must leave it to the man who comes after me." (Ecclesiastes 2:18). The trouble is who gets it next, not what it cost.

Peace is the opposite of what he finds, friend. The text says, "So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 2:20). Despair, not peace. Thinking it over made it heavier for him.

False is right, baker. The Teacher says, "…my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 2:20). Despair, not peace. So the verse says the opposite of finding peace.

Evil is the word, friend. When a man who labored with wisdom, knowledge and skill must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, the Teacher says "…this too is futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). He puts that label on it himself. I think it's a hard verse to read.

Mystery sounds gentler, baker, but that's not his word. He says a man's portion going to someone who has not worked for it is "…futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). I think he's bothered by it. Still, the word he actually uses is evil.
A test would at least have a purpose, friend, but the Teacher doesn't call it that. He says this is "…futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). No reason is given here, just the hurt of it.
Mind it is, baker. The Teacher says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Even at night, the mind keeps going. The verse names the mind as what does not rest.

You'd think tired hands would finally get a rest, friend. But the verse says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Hands aren't mentioned there. It's the mind that does not rest.
His household isn't mentioned in this verse, baker. The Teacher says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). The trouble named is his mind. It isn't the people around him.

explanations.answer: To eat and drink and enjoy his work
explanations.explanation: That's the turn, friend. After all that heaviness, the Teacher says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Simple things, taken as they come. I think the room gets a little lighter right here.

explanations.answer: To gather more than anyone before him
explanations.explanation: Gathering isn't what he calls better, baker. He says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Piling up more isn't part of that. Enjoying the work is.

explanations.answer: To grow wiser than all his neighbors
explanations.explanation: He already tried wisdom, friend, and asked what it gained him (Ecclesiastes 2:15). So that's not his answer. He says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24).

True, baker. The Teacher says, "I have also seen that this is from the hand of God." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Eating, drinking and enjoying your work are not something you squeeze out alone. They come from God's hand.

It's actually true, friend. Right after saying nothing is better than to eat and drink and enjoy his work, the Teacher adds, "I have also seen that this is from the hand of God." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). He's saying where the enjoyment comes from.

explanations.answer: Gathering what he'll hand to one who pleases God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says, "…to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God." (Ecclesiastes 2:26). The sinner gathers, and what he gathers is handed over to one who pleases God. That's the task the Teacher names for the sinner, set beside the wisdom, knowledge and joy God gives the one who pleases Him.

explanations.answer: Guarding the gates of Jerusalem through the night
explanations.explanation: Gate duty isn't anywhere in this verse, friend. The text says the sinner's task is "…gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God." (Ecclesiastes 2:26). The job is gathering, not guarding.

explanations.answer: Rebuilding the ruined walls of his own city
explanations.explanation: No walls to rebuild here, baker. The Teacher says God assigns the sinner "…the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God." (Ecclesiastes 2:26). It's all about gathering and handing over.
